title: Midnight songs (Acts 16:16–40)
hook: a slave girl freed, a beating, prison, hymns, an earthquake, a jailer baptized
tomorrow: who checks a preacher's homework, and why does Acts praise them?

segments.voice: By the river in Philippi, a few women prayed, and the Lord opened her heart: Lydia's. Same city, some days on, and the welcome runs out.
screen: `THE LORD OPENED HER HEART.` → `SAME CITY, HARDER DAYS.`

segments.voice: Three in the morning is the loneliest hour for a worried mind. Some people scroll. Some pace the kitchen. In Philippi, Paul sets a slave girl free from the spirit her owners profited from, and they see "that the hope of their gains was gone." So Paul and Silas are dragged before the magistrates, beaten, and locked in the inner prison, feet fastened in the stocks. And at midnight? "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." They sing.
screen: `THE LONELIEST HOUR.` → `BEATEN, FEET IN THE STOCKS.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THEY SING.`

segments.voice: Then an earthquake. The doors open, every prisoner's bands come loose, and the jailer, sure his prisoners have fled, is about to harm himself. Paul calls out in the dark: "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here." He brings a light, comes in trembling, and asks, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Before dawn the jailer has washed their wounds and fed them at his own table, and his household is baptized. If a dark hour like that is yours right now, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. So is singing the faithful thing in a hard hour? Christians hold two honest views. The first: yes. Praise in the dark is faith at its bravest, and the other prisoners heard it. Paul later writes, "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." The second: not always, and not on command. The Bible keeps sad songs too. In Psalm 137, exiles say, "We hanged our harps upon the willows," and ask, "How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?" Christians who hold this view say lament is prayer too, and forced cheer can bury real grief. Here's the detail both sides can use: Acts never says what they sang. It says they prayed and sang. The hurt and the song, in the same cell.
screen: `DO THYSELF NO HARM.` · `VIEW ONE: PRAISE IN THE DARK.` · `VIEW TWO: HARPS ON THE WILLOWS.` · `PRAYED AND SANG, SAME CELL.` · then, large: `AT MIDNIGHT THEY SANG.`

segments.voice: Hum or sing one line of a song you know by heart, softly, once or a few times, in whatever key the day is in: glad, tired or sad. It doesn't need to sound good; it only needs to be yours. If singing isn't for you, listen to the room instead, the way the prisoners listened.
Midnight songs. Paul and Silas, beaten and locked in the stocks, praying and singing while the prisoners listened.
The line to keep: at midnight they sang, before anything at all had changed. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians sing hymns and psalms in hard hours as well as glad ones, at home, at bedsides and in church, and some churches also pray the psalms of lament.

fork.setup: your choir is asked to sing the week a classmate died. one alto wants only bright, hopeful songs. another wants a sad psalm. what's the best case for the sad one?
options: grief sung honestly is still prayer; the Bible keeps those songs.
sad songs show the singers have quietly given up on God.
Paul and Silas sang only cheerful songs, so sad ones are a break.
fork.reveal: that's the lament view at its best: Psalm 137 is in the Bible too. the praise view answers with a midnight cell. both are Christian voices.

original.note: Greek: they sang praises, the verb in Acts 16:25.

trapdoor: what you thought: the songs opened the prison doors.
what it means: Acts says an earthquake opened the doors; the songs were already rising, and the prisoners heard them.
what a scholar hears: next morning Paul says they are Romans, beaten openly uncondemned, and asks the magistrates to come and bring them out themselves (Acts 16:37).
guess: songs sung in a prison cell at the darkest hour
hymns written for a Christmas midnight service
night songs the temple guards sang on watch

chat.says: choir sings sunday & i'm on the solo. nia still won't talk. singing happy stuff feels fake rn.
options: Paul and Silas sang at midnight, sore and locked up. A song can be honest and still be praise.
Then don't sing. The Bible says you can't sing the Lord's song when you're feeling sad.
Just fake it. Paul and Silas only sang once the earthquake had already set them free.
chat.meaning: Acts says they prayed and sang at midnight, before anything changed. A song in a hard hour can hold the hurt and the praise together.

Silas.meaning: Paul's traveling companion, locked up with him

magistrates.meaning: the city officials who judged them

stocks.meaning: a wooden frame that locked a prisoner's feet

notes: For parents: this lesson includes a beating and the jailer about to harm himself. Acts 16:27 says he drew his sword and would have killed himself; the lesson softens this to 'is about to harm himself', keeps Paul's 'Do thyself no harm', and adds a crisis line (988 in the US, or local emergency help). Confirm the wording.
'The spirit her owners profited from' paraphrases 'a spirit of divination' and 'soothsaying' (16:16). Confirm.
'Before dawn' follows 'the same hour of the night' (16:33) and 'when it was day' (16:35). Confirm.

v3 debate shape: two views inside Christianity, praise in the dark (Acts 16:25; Philippians 4:4) and lament as prayer (Psalm 137), each given its best case; 'both are Christian voices'. Confirm both are fairly stated and neither is ranked.

'Paul later writes' Philippians 4:4: Philippians is among the letters scholars generally hold Paul wrote, and it is addressed to the church at Philippi. The lesson doesn't claim the link to this night. Confirm.
Psalm 137:4 quoted with the KJV's capitals ('LORD'S'); confirm the exact form.
howItsDone: 'some churches also pray the psalms of lament' is a general practice claim; confirm.
